q: On moving down a group of the periodic table, atomic radius generally:
o: Stays the same, because the outer configuration is the same
Increases, because a new electron shell is added in each period
x: Each step down a group adds a new shell, so the outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and the atom is larger, despite the higher nuclear charge.

q: Atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period mainly because:
o: A new shell is added for each element
Shielding by inner electrons increases sharply
Nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell
Atomic mass increases across the period
x: Across a period the proton number rises but the electrons go into the same shell, with little extra shielding. The stronger pull draws the shell closer.

q: Which comparison of radii is correct?
x: Adding an electron increases repulsion and expands the electron cloud, so an anion is larger than its atom. A cation is smaller than its atom.

q: O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ all have 10 electrons. Which of these ions is the smallest?
x: In an isoelectronic series the ion with the most protons pulls the same 10 electrons in most strongly. Mg²⁺ has 12 protons, the most here, so it is smallest; O²⁻ (8 protons) is largest.

q: The Cl–Cl bond length in a chlorine molecule is 198 pm. The covalent radius of chlorine is:
x: Covalent radius is half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms joined by a single covalent bond: 198/2 = 99 pm.

q: Which equation represents the first ionisation energy of sodium?
x: Ionisation energy is the energy to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of isolated gaseous atoms. Starting from the solid adds atomisation; adding an electron is electron affinity.

q: The first ionisation energy of magnesium is higher than that of aluminium because:
o: Aluminium has a smaller nuclear charge than magnesium
Magnesium has more electron shells than aluminium
The electron removed from magnesium is a 3p electron
The electron removed from aluminium is a 3p electron, higher in energy and more shielded than magnesium's 3s electron
x: Mg is [Ne]3s² and Al is [Ne]3s²3p¹. The single 3p electron of Al is higher in energy and partly shielded by the 3s pair, so it is removed more easily.

q: The second ionisation energy of sodium is much greater than its first because the second electron:
o: Is removed from the same 3s orbital as the first electron
Is added to the atom rather than removed
Is removed from a filled inner shell, closer to the nucleus, and from a positive ion
Is removed from a larger, neutral atom
x: Na is [Ne]3s¹. After the 3s electron goes, the next one must come from the full 2p subshell of Na⁺, which is much closer to the nucleus and held strongly.

q: Which element has the most negative (highest) electron affinity?
x: Chlorine releases the most energy on gaining an electron. Fluorine's value is a little lower because its very small 2p shell causes strong repulsion with the incoming electron.

q: Which statement about the carbon–carbon bonds in ethane, ethene and ethyne is correct?
o: The C–C bond is the shortest and the strongest
The C≡C bond is the longest and the weakest
The C≡C bond is the shortest and the strongest
All three bonds have the same length and energy
x: More shared electron pairs pull the atoms closer, so bond length falls and bond energy rises from C–C to C=C to C≡C. Shorter bonds are generally stronger.

q: Which order of electronegativity is correct?
x: Electronegativity increases across a period as nuclear charge rises and size falls. Fluorine is the most electronegative element of all.

q: The s-block of the periodic table consists of:
o: Groups I and II (alkali and alkaline earth metals)
x: In s-block elements the last electron enters an s orbital; these are Groups I and II. Groups 13 to 18 form the p-block, groups 3 to 12 the d-block.

q: An element has the configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p³. It belongs to the:
x: The block is set by the subshell receiving the last electron. Here the last electrons enter 4p, so it is a p-block element (arsenic, Group V).

q: In the f-block elements, the last electron enters:
x: The f-block (lanthanides and actinides) fills the 4f and 5f subshells. The (n−1)d subshell is filled in the d-block.

q: In the d-block (transition) elements, the last electron enters the:
x: In the fourth period, for example, the 3d subshell fills after 4s, so the differentiating electron goes into the (n−1)d subshell.

q: The element with atomic number 20 is in:
x: Z = 20 is calcium, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s². The last electron is in 4s, so it is in the s-block, period 4, Group II.

q: The element with atomic number 26 is in:
x: Z = 26 is iron, [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Its outermost shell is n = 4 and the last electron enters 3d, so it is a d-block element of period 4.

q: The element with atomic number 35 belongs to:
x: Z = 35 is bromine, [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁵. Seven outer electrons (4s² 4p⁵) give Group VIIA, the n = 4 shell gives period 4, and the last electron in 4p gives the p-block.

q: The general outer electronic configuration of p-block elements is:
x: p-block elements have a filled ns subshell and one to six electrons in np. ns¹⁻² is the s-block and the d and f patterns are the other blocks.

q: Which block contains metals, metalloids and non-metals?
x: The p-block ranges from metals such as Al and Pb, through metalloids such as Si and Ge, to non-metals such as N, O and the halogens. The s-, d- and f-blocks are all metals (apart from hydrogen and helium).

q: Sodium reacts with cold water to give:
x: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. The metal displaces hydrogen from water and leaves an alkaline solution.

q: Which shows the correct order of increasing vigour of reaction with water?
x: Down Group I the atoms get larger and ionisation energy falls, so the outer electron is lost more easily and reaction with water becomes more violent.

q: When sodium burns in excess oxygen, the main product is:
x: Sodium mainly forms sodium peroxide, Na₂O₂, containing the O₂²⁻ ion. Lithium forms the normal oxide Li₂O, and potassium and heavier metals form superoxides.

q: Potassium burns in excess oxygen to form potassium superoxide, KO₂. What is the oxidation number of oxygen in KO₂?
x: K is +1, so the two O atoms together are −1, giving −½ each. This is the superoxide ion O₂⁻; −1 is the value in peroxides and −2 in normal oxides.

q: Lithium burns in oxygen to form only the normal oxide, Li₂O, mainly because:
o: Lithium has the lowest ionisation energy in Group I
The very small Li⁺ ion has high polarising power and cannot stabilise the large peroxide ion
Lithium does not react with oxygen at all
The Li⁺ ion is larger than the other Group I ions
x: Small cations with high charge density distort and destabilise large anions such as O₂²⁻ and O₂⁻. Larger ions like K⁺ can stabilise them, so K forms a superoxide.

q: Which alkali metal reacts directly with nitrogen to form a nitride?
x: Lithium forms Li₃N, an anomalous property it shares with magnesium (diagonal relationship). The other alkali metals do not form nitrides directly.

q: Group I metals (M) react with chlorine to form chlorides with the general formula:
x: Group I metals form M⁺ ions, and chlorine forms Cl⁻, so the chloride is MCl, e.g. 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.

q: Which Group I chloride shows the greatest covalent character?
x: Li⁺ is the smallest Group I ion and polarises the Cl⁻ electron cloud most, so LiCl has some covalent character, e.g. it dissolves in organic solvents.

q: Sodium peroxide is added to ice-cold water. The products are:
x: Na₂O₂ + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂O₂ in cold water. The peroxide ion takes H⁺ to give H₂O₂; hydrogen gas is given by the metal, not the peroxide.

q: What volume of hydrogen at STP is produced when 2.3 g of sodium reacts completely with water? (Na = 23; 1 mol gas = 22.4 dm³)
x: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Moles of Na = 2.3/23 = 0.1, giving 0.05 mol H₂ = 0.05 × 22.4 = 1.12 dm³. Ignoring the 2 : 1 ratio gives 2.24 dm³.

q: Potassium reacts with water more vigorously than sodium because potassium:
o: Has a higher nuclear charge, which holds its outer electron more tightly
Has two outer electrons while sodium has one
Forms a protective oxide layer that sodium lacks
Has a larger atom and a lower ionisation energy, so it loses its outer electron more easily
x: The outer 4s electron of K is farther from the nucleus and better shielded than the 3s electron of Na, so it is removed more easily and K reacts faster.

q: When magnesium is heated in steam, the products are:
x: Mg + H₂O(g) → MgO + H₂. Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water but readily with steam.

q: Which Group II element is the least reactive towards water?
x: Reactivity with water increases down Group II. Beryllium is the least reactive (the FSc book says it does not react even with steam), magnesium reacts with hot water or steam, and calcium and barium react with cold water.

q: Calcium reacts with cold water to form:
x: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂. The hydrogen bubbles off and the solution becomes alkaline (limewater).

q: Which shows the correct order of increasing reactivity of Group II metals with water?
x: Reactivity rises down Group II as atoms get larger and the two outer electrons are lost more easily.

q: On heating in excess oxygen, which metal forms a peroxide, MO₂?
x: The large Ba²⁺ ion can stabilise the peroxide ion, so barium forms BaO₂. Beryllium and magnesium form normal oxides, and lithium forms Li₂O.

q: When magnesium ribbon burns in air, the products are:
x: Magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame, reacting with oxygen to give MgO and with nitrogen of the air to give Mg₃N₂.

q: Which Group II chloride is covalent, has a low melting point and forms polymeric chains in the solid?
x: The tiny Be²⁺ ion has very high polarising power, so BeCl₂ is covalent. The chlorides lower in the group are ionic solids.

q: Which Group II oxide is amphoteric?
x: BeO reacts with both acids and bases. The other Group II oxides are basic, and their basic strength increases down the group.

q: What volume of hydrogen at STP is produced when 4 g of calcium reacts completely with water? (Ca = 40; 1 mol gas = 22.4 dm³)
x: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂. Moles of Ca = 4/40 = 0.1, giving 0.1 mol H₂ = 2.24 dm³. Using the 2 of water as if it applied to H₂ gives 4.48 dm³.

q: Which property is shared by lithium and magnesium (diagonal relationship)?
o: Both form peroxides when burnt in excess oxygen
Both react explosively with cold water
Both burn in air to form a nitride as well as a normal oxide
Both show a valency of two in their compounds
x: Li and Mg both form Li₃N and Mg₃N₂ besides the normal oxides Li₂O and MgO. Neither forms peroxides readily, both react only slowly with cold water, and Li has valency one.

q: The outer electronic configuration of Group IV elements is:
x: C, Si, Ge, Sn and Pb all have four outer electrons, arranged as ns² np². This gives them a group valency of four.

q: Which two Group IV elements are metalloids?
x: Group IV changes from the non-metal carbon, through the metalloids silicon and germanium, to the metals tin and lead.

q: Because of the inert pair effect, the more stable oxidation state of lead is:
x: Down Group IV the ns² pair becomes less willing to take part in bonding, so the lower state (+2) becomes more stable. For lead +2 is more stable than +4.

q: Which statement is correct?
o: PbO₂ is an oxidising agent, because Pb(+4) tends to change to the more stable +2 state
SnCl₂ is an oxidising agent, because Sn(+2) tends to change to the +4 state
PbO₂ is a reducing agent, because Pb(+4) tends to change to +2
PbCl₂ is a strong oxidising agent, because +2 is unstable for lead
x: Pb(+4) gains electrons to become Pb(+2), so PbO₂ oxidises other substances. For tin, +4 is more stable, so SnCl₂ loses electrons and acts as a reducing agent.

q: Which of these oxides of Group IV elements is amphoteric?
x: PbO reacts with both acids and alkalis. CO₂ and SiO₂ are acidic oxides, and CO is a neutral oxide.

q: Carbon dioxide is a gas but silicon dioxide is a hard solid with a high melting point because:
o: SiO₂ is an ionic compound, while CO₂ is covalent
Silicon forms strong double bonds with oxygen, while carbon cannot
SiO₂ is a giant covalent network, while CO₂ exists as small separate molecules
CO₂ has hydrogen bonding between its molecules
x: Carbon forms C=O double bonds giving discrete O=C=O molecules held by weak forces. Silicon does not form such double bonds, so each Si links to four O atoms in a 3-D network.

q: SiCl₄ is readily hydrolysed by water, but CCl₄ is not. The main reason is that:
o: The C–Cl bond is much more polar than the Si–Cl bond
CCl₄ is an ionic compound that does not dissolve in water
Silicon has vacant d orbitals that can accept lone pairs from water, but carbon has none
Silicon is more electronegative than carbon
x: Water's lone pair can attack Si through its empty 3d orbitals, starting hydrolysis. Carbon has no d orbitals in its valence shell and is crowded by four Cl atoms.

q: Silicon tetrachloride reacts with water to give:
x: SiCl₄ + 4H₂O → Si(OH)₄ + 4HCl. The HCl formed gives white fumes in moist air; silicic acid can lose water to give silica.

q: Which tetrachloride is the least stable, decomposing on gentle warming into the dichloride and chlorine?
x: PbCl₄ → PbCl₂ + Cl₂ on warming, because the +2 state is more stable for lead (inert pair effect). The other tetrachlorides are stable.

q: Which Group IV element shows the greatest tendency for catenation?
x: Carbon forms long chains and rings of C–C bonds because the C–C bond is strong. The tendency falls sharply down the group.
